n: Two days after the joyful feast ends, the people gather again — this time to fast and mourn their sins. Sackcloth and dirt on the head were signs of deep humility and sorrow.

f.g: Rough garments of goat’s hair worn in mourning or repentance.

n: They separate themselves from foreigners for this covenant renewal and confess not only their own sins but their ancestors’ too.

f.g: Foreigners who were not part of Israel’s covenant.

f.w: confessed their sins, and the iniquities of their fathers

n: For about three hours they read scripture, and for another three they confessed and worshipped. Study and repentance went hand in hand.

f.w: one fourth part of the day
f.g: About three hours of a twelve-hour day.

n: Levites stand on a raised platform and cry out loudly to God, leading the people in prayer.

f.g: A raised platform or steps from which leaders could be seen and heard.

n: The Levites call everyone to stand and praise God forever. The long prayer that follows (verses 6–38) is one of the great prayers of the Bible, retelling Israel’s whole history.

f.w: Stand up and bless the LORD your God

n: The prayer begins with creation: the Lord alone made the heavens, earth, and seas, and keeps them alive. Even the heavenly hosts worship Him.

f.g: The highest heavens.

n: God chose Abram, brought him out of Ur, and gave him a new name, Abraham — “father of many nations.” A new name marked a new covenant identity.
God found Abraham faithful and covenanted to give his descendants the land of Canaan — and He kept His word. The point: God is righteous and keeps His promises.
God saw Israel’s suffering in Egypt and heard their cry at the Red Sea.

f.w: didst see the affliction of our fathers

n: God sent plagues on Pharaoh because Egypt treated Israel arrogantly. Through these wonders, God made His name known in all the earth.

f.g: Acted arrogantly and cruelly.

n: God parted the Red Sea for Israel to cross on dry ground, then drowned their pursuers like a stone dropped into deep water.

f.w: as a stone into the mighty waters

n: God led them by a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night — constant, visible guidance.
At Sinai God came down and spoke from heaven, giving them good and true laws. The law was a gift, not a burden.

f.w: camest down also upon mount Sinai

n: He revealed the holy Sabbath and gave commandments through Moses. Interestingly, the Sabbath is singled out — keeping it would become a major issue in Nehemiah 13.
God fed them with manna from heaven and gave water from a rock, and promised them the land. Jesus later called Himself the true bread from heaven.

f.w: water for them out of the rock

n: But the turning point comes: our ancestors became proud and stubborn and would not listen. The prayer now alternates between God’s kindness and Israel’s rebellion.

f.g: Became stubborn, like an ox refusing to bend its neck to the yoke.

n: They forgot God’s miracles and even chose a leader to take them back to Egyptian slavery. Yet God remained “ready to pardon” — these words echo God’s own self-description to Moses.

f.w: appointed a captain to return to their bondage
a God ready to pardon, gracious and merciful, slow to anger

n: Their worst sin in the wilderness: making a golden calf and calling it the god who saved them from Egypt.

f.g: Acts that provoke or insult God.

n: Even then, God in His mercy did not abandon them. The guiding pillars stayed with them — God’s guidance did not stop because of their failures.

f.g: Many and varied mercies.

n: God also gave His good Spirit to teach them and kept providing manna and water. The Spirit’s role as teacher is a theme Latter-day Saints treasure.

f.w: thy good spirit to instruct them

n: For forty years they lacked nothing; even their clothes didn’t wear out and their feet didn’t swell.

f.g: Grew, became.

n: God gave them victory over the kingdoms east of the Jordan, including Sihon and Og, and divided the land among them.

f.g: Allot them land region by region; or, assign every corner of the land.

n: God multiplied Israel as the stars, fulfilling His promise to Abraham, and brought them into the land.
Under Joshua, Israel entered and took the land, and God gave them victory over the Canaanites.

f.g: Brought under control; defeated.

n: They received cities, rich farmland, homes already furnished, wells, vineyards, and orchards. They ate and “became fat” — prosperity that would soon lead to pride.
Yet they rebelled, threw God’s law behind their backs, and killed the prophets who called them to repent. The same pattern of prosperity leading to pride appears often in the Book of Mormon.

f.w: cast thy law behind their backs
f.g: Treated it with contempt, ignored it.

n: So God let enemies oppress them, but when they cried out, He sent “saviours” — the judges — to rescue them. This describes the cycle of the book of Judges.

f.g: Oppressed, harassed.

n: Once at peace, they sinned again, and the cycle repeated: sin, suffering, crying out, rescue. God delivered them “many times.”

f.w: after they had rest, they did evil again

n: God warned them to return to His law, which gives life to those who keep it. But they turned away like a stubborn ox shrugging off its yoke.

f.w: which if a man do, he shall live in them

f.g: Pulled away from the yoke — refused to carry the load.

n: For many years God patiently sent His Spirit through the prophets, but the people would not listen. Finally they were handed over to foreign nations — Assyria and Babylon.

f.g: Be patient with, hold back from punishing.

f.w: by thy spirit in thy prophets

n: Yet even in judgment, God did not destroy them completely or abandon them, because He is gracious and merciful. Every part of this history ends in mercy.
Now the prayer turns to the present: Great and faithful God, don’t treat our suffering as small — the troubles that have come on everyone since the Assyrian invasions.

f.w: the great, the mighty, and the terrible God

f.g: Assyria destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel about 722 BC.

n: The people admit God was fair in everything that happened; they were the ones who did wrong. Accepting responsibility is the turning point of repentance.

f.w: thou art just in all that is brought upon us

n: No group was innocent — not kings, princes, priests, or ancestors. Everyone ignored God’s warnings.

f.g: God’s solemn warnings and commands.

n: Even when they had their own kingdom and a rich land, they did not serve God or turn from evil.
The painful irony: in the very land God gave their fathers to enjoy, they are now servants of a foreign king.
The land’s harvest goes to Persian kings in taxes, and the rulers control even their bodies and livestock. They are in great distress.

f.w: they have dominion over our bodies
f.g: Persian kings could draft their labor and soldiers.

n: Because of all this, they make a firm written covenant, sealed by their leaders. Confession leads to commitment — the details follow in chapter 10.

f.g: A firm, binding agreement.
Put their official seals on the document as witnesses.
